v.why: Raising an already large Adam step pushes training into divergence, producing large accuracy drops (e.g. exp 72, 76, 79).
At tiny learning rates the network underfits in 243 epochs, so a larger step helps (exp 70, 73).
Deeper networks are less stable at high learning rates, so adding a layer there hurts badly (exp 48, 58, 60).
With slow learning, extra depth adds capacity and gradient paths that speed fitting (exp 47, 52).
Raising an already strong L2 penalty over-regularizes the network and accuracy collapses (exp 11, 16, 20).
Large batches give fewer, less noisy updates, so they tolerate and benefit from larger steps (exp 65, 73).
Small, noisy batches combined with a larger step size destabilize training (exp 72).
Wider layers speed optimization when learning is slow, giving consistent gains (exp 88, 93).
At high learning rates, larger batches reduce gradient noise and rescue unstable training (exp 27, 39, 32).
At low learning rates, larger batches cut the number of updates and worsen underfitting (exp 26, 33).

raw:
I based these on the 100 single-seed experiments and on how MLPs trained with Adam usually behave. The clearest pattern is around learning rate. Training becomes unstable at high learning rates. Very low learning rates mean the model underfits, so increasing capacity, step size or update count helps there. A heavy L2 penalty causes collapse.
